title: How can we fill the boxes in two different ways?
description: Two boxes multiplied must give two point four, and another pair of boxes must give fourteen point five. The video starts from a whole number fact for the digits, then puts the decimal places back by counting, to fill each pair of boxes in two ways.
teaching_notes: One idea: find a whole number fact for the digits of the product, then give the right number of decimal places to the factors. Ask the class for any two numbers that multiply to twenty four before any work is shown. Watch for students who put a decimal place in the product but forget to put it back in a factor.

source: End of chapter Figure it Out, Q7
video_script.why: The child takes the digits of a product from a known fact and counts decimal places, and now works backwards from a product to the factors.
video_script.substitution: A whole number fact gives the digits, and the decimal places of the product are shared out among the factors.
video_script.anchor: Two products with empty boxes: box times box equals 2.4, and box times box equals 14.5
video_script.payoff_line: Here are two ways to fill the boxes for each product

final_answer.value: (a) for example 1.2 × 2 and 0.6 × 4 (b) for example 2.9 × 5 and 1.45 × 10
final_answer.spoken: one point two times two and zero point six times four, then two point nine times five and one point four five times ten

maths_rules: 2.4 has one decimal place; 24 = 12 x 2, so 1.2 x 2 = 2.4 (1 + 0 = 1 place)
14.5 has one decimal place; 145 = 29 x 5, so 2.9 x 5 = 14.5 (1 + 0 = 1 place)
video_script.design: One idea: a whole number fact gives the digits, then the decimal places go back into a factor. The two products with empty boxes stay on the board all video; the working band shows two ways for the first product, two for the second, and a check by counting places.

<bookmark mark='first'/>Two boxes are multiplied to give two point four.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Two more boxes are multiplied to give fourteen point five.
Fill the boxes in at least two different ways for each. What numbers can go in?

narration: <bookmark mark='tenths'/>Two point four is twenty four tenths, so its digits are two and four.

<bookmark mark='rule'/>Then we count decimal places to put the point back, as we did with a known product.

narration: <bookmark mark='why'/>Step one, the first product, way one.
<bookmark mark='place'/>Two point four has one decimal place.
<bookmark mark='fact'/>Twenty four is twelve times two.
<bookmark mark='put'/>Put the one decimal place into the twelve, and leave the two as it is.

beats.on_screen: Step 2, first product, way two: 24 = 6 × 4; put 1 decimal place in the 6

marks.put: an arrow shows one decimal place going into the 6

narration: <bookmark mark='fact'/>Step two, the first product, way two. Twenty four is also six times four.
<bookmark mark='put'/>Put the one decimal place into the six, and leave the four as it is.

beats.on_screen: Step 3, second product, way one: 14.5 has 1 decimal place; 145 = 29 × 5; put 1 decimal place in the 29

marks.why: the step title and 14.5 are lit

narration: <bookmark mark='why'/>Step three, the second product, way one.
<bookmark mark='place'/>Fourteen point five has one decimal place.
<bookmark mark='fact'/>One hundred forty five is twenty nine times five.
<bookmark mark='put'/>Put the one decimal place into the twenty nine, and leave the five as it is.

beats.on_screen: Step 4, second product, way two: 14.5 = 14.50 has 2 decimal places; 145 × 10 = 1450; put 2 decimal places in the 145

marks.two: 14.5 is rewritten as 14.50 with 2 decimal places
marks.put: an arrow shows two decimal places going into the 145

narration: <bookmark mark='two'/>Step four, the second product, way two. Write fourteen point five as fourteen point five zero, with two decimal places.
<bookmark mark='fact'/>One hundred forty five times ten is one thousand four hundred fifty.
<bookmark mark='put'/>Put the two decimal places into the one hundred forty five, and leave the ten as it is.

beats.on_screen: Step 5: check the places: 1 + 0 = 1 for 2.4 and for 14.5; 2 + 0 = 2 for 14.50

marks.one: 1 + 0 = 1 is written for the first two ways
marks.two: 2 + 0 = 2 is written for the last way

narration: <bookmark mark='one'/>Step five, check the decimal places. One plus none is one place, which matches two point four and fourteen point five.
<bookmark mark='two'/>Two plus none is two places, which matches fourteen point five zero.

marks.ans: the boxes are filled and boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Here are two ways to fill the boxes for each product.
<bookmark mark='first'/>For two point four, one point two times two, and zero point six times four.
<bookmark mark='second'/>For fourteen point five, two point nine times five, and one point four five times ten.
